Jozadak
JOZ-uh-dak
proper noun
Hebrew Yotsadaq (H3136), the LORD is righteous — from Yah, the covenant name, and tsadaq (H6663), to be righteous, to be just; the fuller form is Jehozadak.

Biblical Definition

Jozadak, also written Jehozadak, was the high priest's son who went into captivity when Nebuchadnezzar carried Judah away, and the father of Jeshua the high priest who came back. He himself never ministered in a standing temple: the house was burned before his turn came, and he died in Babylon. His son is named again and again in the record of the return — Jeshua the son of Jozadak raising the altar, beginning the house, and standing under Haggai's preaching (Ezr 3:8; 5:2; 10:18; Neh 12:26). The name means the LORD is righteous, and a man bearing it watched the sanctuary he was born to serve go up in smoke for his nation's sin. That is the confession Scripture puts in the mouth of the exiles themselves. The LORD is righteous; for I have rebelled against his commandment (Lam 1:18); O Lord, righteousness belongeth unto thee, but unto us confusion of faces (Dan 9:7). Judah did not go into Babylon protesting her innocence. She went confessing that the God who judged her had done right, and the priestly line carried that verdict in its very name across seventy years until a son of Jozadak stood again at an altar in Jerusalem.

Origin & Era

Son of Seraiah the high priest, carried into Babylon; father of Jeshua the high priest of the return. His name means the LORD is righteous.

JOZADAK, Hebrew Yotsadaq, the LORD is righteous; also written Jehozadak.

Of the high-priestly line of Aaron through Eleazar and Phinehas.

He went into captivity when the LORD carried away Judah by the hand of Nebuchadnezzar.

Father of Jeshua, the high priest who returned with Zerubbabel.

Named repeatedly in Ezra and Nehemiah in the phrase Jeshua the son of Jozadak.

Key Scripture

Ezr 3:8 — "Now in the second year of their coming unto the house of God at Jerusalem, in the second month, began Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, and Jeshua the son of Jozadak, and the remnant of their brethren the priests and the Levites, and all they that were come out of the captivity unto Jerusalem; and appointed the Levites, from twenty years old and upward, to set forward the work of the house of the LORD."

Ezr 5:2 — "Then rose up Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, and Jeshua the son of Jozadak, and began to build the house of God which is at Jerusalem: and with them were the prophets of God helping them."

Ezr 10:18 — "And among the sons of the priests there were found that had taken strange wives: namely, of the sons of Jeshua the son of Jozadak, and his brethren; Maaseiah, and Eliezer, and Jarib, and Gedaliah."

Neh 12:26 — "These were in the days of Joiakim the son of Jeshua, the son of Jozadak, and in the days of Nehemiah the governor, and of Ezra the priest, the scribe."

Modern Corruption

The exile is read as a political misfortune; Scripture presents it as the righteous judgment of God, confessed as such by the exiles themselves.

expand to see more

It is common to explain the Babylonian captivity purely in the terms of ancient geopolitics — a small kingdom caught between empires, destroyed by the ordinary machinery of conquest, its religious literature written afterward to make theological sense of a defeat. The prophets who lived through it will not have it. They had said for a century what would come and why: because ye have not heard my words, behold, I will send and take all the families of the north… and will bring them against this land (Jer 25:8-9). Nebuchadnezzar was the instrument; the hand was the LORD's, and the cause was covenant treachery.

What makes the exilic confession remarkable is that the victims agreed with the verdict. Daniel, who had done nothing to deserve Babylon, prayed O Lord, righteousness belongeth unto thee, but unto us confusion of faces (Dan 9:7) and numbered himself with the guilty. That is repentance as Scripture defines it: not the admission that things went badly, but the confession that God was right. The principle to recover is that a people who can say the LORD is righteous over their own ruin are the only people positioned to be restored, because they have stopped disputing the diagnosis.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Yotsadaq (H3136), from the covenant name Yah and tsadaq (H6663), to be just, to be righteous.

expand to see more

Hebrew tsadaq (H6663) — to be righteous, to be just, to be declared in the right; the root of justification.

Hebrew Yotsadaq (H3136) — the LORD is righteous; father of Jeshua the high priest, Ezra 3:8, 5:2, 10:18, Nehemiah 12:26.

Hebrew tsedeq (H6664) — righteousness, rightness; the LORD our righteousness (Jer 23:6).

Hebrew Yehotsadaq (H3087) — the fuller form of the name, used in 1 Chronicles 6:14-15 and in Haggai and Zechariah.

Greek dikaios (G1342) — just, righteous; that he might be just, and the justifier of him which believeth in Jesus (Rom 3:26).

Usage

"“Jeshua the son of Jozadak” — the phrase that carries his memory."

"“The LORD is righteous; for I have rebelled against his commandment” (Lam 1:18)."

"“Then rose up Zerubbabel… and Jeshua the son of Jozadak, and began to build the house of God”."
